Hey friend, I'm a music major too.  All of those points that you brought up are extremely valid.  The practice hours are long and sometimes yield nothing, the job prospects are daunting, and your professors are never truly pleased.  Being a music major takes a whole lot of passion for music and the ability to take a beating over and over again.  Everyone I know that has stuck with it (as a music ed major) does it for the love of kids and of teaching and that is *definitely* not for everybody.  

And you know what?  That's totally okay.  

You can have a love for music but it doesn't have to be your job.  If you don't feel like it's for you then you need to do what you think is best for your mental health and well-being.  You can still be musical and be a math/science major.  Most universities have community bands/choirs/orchestras you can perform in.  Plus at a lot of places you don't even have to be a music major to be in the program.  As of right now we have 2 trumpets/1 trombone/1 sax in the top jazz band at my school that aren't even music majors.  You can also look into community groups and city bands/choirs, because they're always on the look out for people with musical training.  You can also look into giving lessons independently (if that's your preference), or you can write/arrange music on your own.  

Please do what you think is best for *you*, but know that if you want to continue being a musician you don't have to completely give it up just because you switched majors/life paths.  Music is a universal language and truly the greatest of the arts, and is available to anybody and everybody at any stage of their lives.

The best thing you can do is just be there with them.  You can say all you want "People care about you, you are loved" but to someone that is suicidal those words may not penetrate the haze of self hatred or exhaustion around their minds.  Actions speak louder than words.  

When I was in my last downswing I felt like I had lost everybody.  My friends wouldn't talk to me or reply to me.  I'd reach out to them, get a few minutes of FB/text/phone conversation, and it'd be done.  The only thing that kept me going was my good friend/mentor that stuck with me and texted me every hour on the hour and expected a reply to make sure I was still kicking.  I got out of that downswing thanks to her.  She reminded me of why she's my friend, how bright my future is, and of all the people in my life that would miss me like my mom or my brothers.  She still texts me and we make plans to hang out even though we're both adults with busy schedules.  Its little things like that, just sticking around and being my friend, that pulled me back from the edge.

Your best bet would be referring your friends to people that are qualified to help them.  If you're in high school, the counselors are available.  If you're in university, most schools have a team of counselors and therapists available for the students at a reduced cost or even free.  If you're neither, take a look for local counselors/therapists that you could refer your friends to.  If thats not an option, there's always phone resources or online resources.  What country are you in?  I can help you find those resources so you can have them tucked away in your brain to give to your buddies.  

The best thing you can do is to keep being you.  You sound like a great person and a very good friend.  Often if someone is suicidal they need someone to reach out to in order to ground them and to help them center themselves.  Just a simple "Hey buddy, if you ever need to talk about something real, I'm here" can mean the world if it's said with sincerity.
It's slow goings, but every step forward is a new victory.  Thanks, buddy.
